findings.title: Exhausted user-storage recovery codes are not removed
findings.body: After a successful recovery-code login, the authenticator now loads the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers the user-storage credential. If that model reports all codes used, it still calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes credentials stored in Keycloak's local credential store, not a credential owned by a user storage provider. The storage credential therefore stays configured, isConfiguredFor remains true, and the next login still demands a recovery code even though none are left. If recovery codes are the only second factor, the user cannot get back in to satisfy the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES action that is added on the same path. Disable or update the credential through the storage SPI (disableCredentialType / updateCredential) when the federated credential is exhausted.

findings.title: Login form assumes storage returns a hashed recovery-code model
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential writes the user-storage credential as a UserCredentialModel whose value is a JSON array of plaintext codes, not RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData/SecretData. The login bean (and the authenticator after a successful check) then calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on whatever getFederatedCredentialsStream returns. A storage provider that persists and returns the value it was given has null or non-model secretData, so createFromCredentialModel throws and the recovery-code page fails with a server error before the user can sign in. Only the test provider hides this by rebuilding a model with createFromValues inside getCredentials. Keycloak needs a defined, converted representation (or must not parse storage credentials as local secret data) or user-storage recovery codes cannot be challenged.

findings.title: Storage recovery codes are reusable and never advance
findings.body: isValid deserializes the stored JSON list and returns true if any code equals the input. It does not require the next code in sequence, remove the used code, or update the stored credential. getCredentials then calls createFromValues on the original list, which hashes every code, resets the next index to the first code, and assigns a new credential id on every read. disableCredentialType also ignores recovery-authn-codes, so the credential cannot be turned off. The new login test only submits code 0 once, so it stays green while this provider treats backup codes as a reusable shared secret and cannot drive the all-codes-used path. Consume the matched code in isValid, return a stable id and the remaining sequence from getCredentials, and clear the credential in disableCredentialType.
